fields.name: Malware Infection Response - Updated
fields.description: Malware incidents are among the most common cybersecurity threats faced by organisations today. In this category, you will practise the NIST Incident Response framework as applied to ransomware, trojans, worms, and spyware outbreaks. Each scenario puts you in the role of an analyst responding to a live infection.
fields.short_summary: Detect, contain, and eradicate malware from compromised systems.

fields.name: Phishing & Social Engineering
fields.description: Phishing remains the top initial access vector in security breaches worldwide. Practise identifying malicious emails, investigating credential theft, responding to spear-phishing campaigns, and educating end-users — all within realistic simulations.
fields.short_summary: Identify, investigate, and mitigate phishing attacks and social engineering attempts.

fields.name: DDoS & Network Disruption
fields.description: Distributed Denial of Service attacks threaten service availability and can be combined with other attack vectors. In this category you will respond to volumetric, protocol, and application-layer attacks — making triage, traffic scrubbing, and ISP escalation decisions.
fields.short_summary: Respond to volumetric attacks, scrub traffic, and restore service availability.

fields.name: Data Breach & Exfiltration
fields.description: Data breaches can expose sensitive customer records, intellectual property, and regulated data. These scenarios develop your skills in breach investigation, forensic log analysis, regulatory notification timelines (GDPR, HIPAA), and post-breach remediation.
fields.short_summary: Investigate data theft, contain the breach, and manage stakeholder communication.

fields.name: Insider Threat Detection
fields.description: Insider threats — whether malicious, negligent, or compromised — are among the hardest incidents to detect. These simulations train you to analyse audit logs, investigate suspicious behaviour, and navigate the legal and HR implications of insider threat investigations.
fields.short_summary: Detect malicious insiders, investigate anomalous access, and protect privileged data.

fields.name: Network Intrusion & APT
fields.description: Advanced Persistent Threat actors are sophisticated, patient, and goal-oriented. These scenarios simulate APT campaigns where you must hunt for indicators of compromise, trace lateral movement, analyse command-and-control traffic, and execute eviction procedures.
fields.short_summary: Hunt advanced persistent threats, analyse lateral movement, and evict intruders.

fields.objective_text: Identify key indicators of a ransomware infection and distinguish them from other malware types.
Apply NIST SP 800-61 containment procedures to stop lateral spread of an active ransomware outbreak.
Evaluate recovery options — paying ransom vs. restoring from backup — and articulate the security implications of each.

fields.title: Monday Morning Alert
fields.situation_text:
It is 08:47 on a Monday. You arrive at the Security Operations Centre at Nexus Financial Services. Before you can pour your coffee, alerts begin firing on the SIEM dashboard.

CRITICAL — Multiple workstations in the Finance department (VLAN 10) have triggered endpoint protection alerts. A quick call to the Help Desk confirms: employees cannot open files, and a text file called "HOW_TO_DECRYPT.txt" has appeared on desktops.

The CISO has been notified. You are the first analyst on-scene. Your first task is to establish the scope of the incident before taking any action.

fields.title: Initial Containment Decision
fields.situation_text:
The SIEM shows 14 workstations in Finance VLAN 10 have been encrypted. Encryption appears to have started at 03:15 this morning — over 5 hours ago.

The malware has NOT yet appeared on other VLANs (HR, IT, Executive).

The CFO is calling you directly asking when systems will be restored. A colleague suggests you should immediately restore from backup to get Finance back online.

What is your FIRST containment action?

fields.title: Identifying the Attack Vector
fields.situation_text:
VLAN 10 has been isolated. The ransomware is no longer spreading.

Your manager asks you to identify how the ransomware entered the network. You pull evidence:

Email logs show a Finance user (alice.white@nexusfinancial.com) received a macro-enabled Excel attachment from an external sender at 03:02 on Sunday night.

VPN logs show a successful authentication at 03:10 from an unfamiliar IP address using alice.white's credentials — before the encryption started.

File server logs confirm the ransomware binary first appeared at 03:14 on the Finance file share.

Based on this evidence, what was the most likely initial infection vector?

fields.title: Eradication and Recovery Approach
fields.situation_text:
The attack chain is confirmed:

1. Phishing email -> macro executes -> credentials harvested
2. Attacker uses stolen VPN credentials to access Finance VLAN
3. Ransomware binary deployed to the Finance file share at 03:14

VLAN 10 remains isolated. The CISO has authorised eradication and recovery.

Your organisation has clean backups from Friday 23:00 (3 days ago). A colleague suggests contacting the attacker to negotiate a cheaper ransom key.

What is the correct eradication and recovery approach?

fields.title: Post-Incident Review & Lessons Learned
fields.situation_text:
The incident has been successfully contained, eradicated, and systems are now recovered. All 14 workstations have been reimaged. Finance VLAN has been brought back online.

LESSONS LEARNED

ATTACK CHAIN: Phishing email -> Macro execution -> Credential theft -> VPN access -> Ransomware deployment

NIST PHASES COMPLETED:
- Preparation: Alert triage and initial scope assessment
- Containment: VLAN isolation to prevent spread
- Detection & Analysis: Attack vector identification from log evidence
- Eradication: Full reimage of all affected workstations
- Recovery: Data restored from Friday backup

REMEDIATION ACTIONS TAKEN:
- alice.white credentials reset and MFA enforced
- Macro execution blocked in Microsoft 365 for Finance users
- Email filtering rules updated to quarantine macro-enabled attachments
- VPN access restricted to known geo-locations
- Backup frequency increased to 4-hour intervals

Excellent work, Analyst. You followed the NIST IR framework correctly under pressure. Your containment decision prevented the ransomware from reaching 4 other VLANs.

Simulation complete. Review your decision log below.

fields.option_text: Isolate VLAN 10 immediately by disabling the inter-VLAN routing on the core switch.
fields.feedback_text: Correct. Network isolation is the highest-priority containment action for an active ransomware outbreak. Disabling inter-VLAN routing prevents the malware from spreading to other segments. Restoring from backup before containment would re-infect clean systems from the still-active malware.

fields.option_text: Begin restoring Finance workstations from last night's backup immediately.
fields.feedback_text: Incorrect. Restoring from backup before the malware is contained will result in immediate re-infection of the restored systems. The ransomware executable is still active in the environment. Containment MUST precede recovery in the NIST IR lifecycle.

fields.option_text: Pay the ransom to get the decryption key and restore operations quickly.
fields.feedback_text: Incorrect. Paying the ransom is strongly discouraged by CISA and the FBI. There is no guarantee the attacker will provide a working decryption key. Payment also funds criminal operations and marks your organisation as a willing payer.

fields.option_text: Take forensic images of all affected drives before touching anything.
fields.feedback_text: Partially correct thinking — forensics is important, but not the FIRST action. With active ransomware spreading across a live network, every minute of delay allows more systems to be encrypted. Isolate first, image later.

fields.option_text: A malicious macro-enabled Excel attachment delivered via a phishing email to a Finance user.
